title: Relations between Tables
summary: Relations answer real questions — user_id is the link that prevents chaos.

sections.heading: Orientation — Lesson Start
sections.subtitle: Lesson Start
sections.contentMarkdown:
- What will you understand? Relations between tables answer real questions — like "this client's conversations" or "this user's files".
- Why now? After designing the tables, they need to be linked — otherwise, the data becomes chaotic and the application gets confused.
- What comes after the lesson? You will design a one-to-many relationship — User → Many Conversations.

sections.heading: Tension — AI Forgets Who It Talks To
sections.subtitle: AI Forgets Who It Talks To
sections.contentMarkdown:
- AI talks to Ahmed then to Sarah — and suddenly sends Sarah a summary of Ahmed's conversation. A privacy disaster.
- The problem: All conversations are in one pile and there is no official link between each conversation and its owner.
- The solution: Separate the tables and link them with a Foreign Key — everything is linked to its owner.

sections.heading: Core Idea — Relations Answer Real Questions
sections.subtitle: Relations Answer Real Questions
sections.contentMarkdown:
- Instead of one table with everything — two tables: `users` and `conversations`. Each conversation has a `user_id` that points to its owner.
- One-to-Many: One client → Many conversations. Each conversation belongs to only one owner.
- The question "Get conversations for client 5" = a relation. Without it, the database does not respond.

sections.heading: Comparison — One Pile vs. Separate and Link
sections.subtitle: One Pile vs. Separate and Link
sections.contentMarkdown:
| Everything in One Table | Two Linked Tables |
|---------------------|----------------|
| `Conversations(client_name, email, message)`. Change the name? Update all messages. Mistake in a letter? New client | `users(id, name)` and `conversations(id, user_id, message)`. Change the name in one place. Each conversation is linked to `user_id` |

sections.heading: Glossary — Two Terms for Linking
sections.subtitle: Two Terms for Linking
sections.contentMarkdown:
| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---------|--------|------|
| Foreign Key | A column in one table that points to `id` in another table — the link between them | `conversations.user_id` → `users.id` |
| One-to-Many | One row in Table A → Many rows in Table B | One client → Many conversations. Each conversation belongs to one owner |

sections.heading: Screenshot Block (Intent)
sections.contentMarkdown: The link between the tables: Imagine `users` = clients and `posts` = conversations. `posts.user_id` = the link that indicates who owns the conversation. Without it, the application is blind.

sections.heading: Quiz — Quick Confirmation
sections.subtitle: Quick Confirmation
sections.contentMarkdown:
Question: Each client (`user`) has many conversations (`conversations`). If the client deletes their account, what is safest for their conversations?
The conversations are deleted with it (Cascade Delete) — to protect their privacy.
The conversations remain and `user_id` becomes empty.
The system refuses to delete the client as long as they have conversations.
Explanation: Cascade Delete protects the client's privacy — no sensitive data after they leave.

sections.heading: Mission — Design a User-to-Many Relationship
sections.subtitle: Design a User-to-Many Relationship
sections.contentMarkdown:
Introduction: Your application has users and each user has many items (conversations, files, tasks). Design the relationship. 10 minutes. Submission: One table, many table, link column (`user_id` → `id`), deletion behavior and why. Evaluation Criteria: | Dimension | Weight | Criteria |
|-------|-------|---------|
| Relationship Design | 70% | `user_id` in the many table; points to `id` in the one table; One-to-Many is clear |
| Deletion Decision | 30% | Behavior when deleting the user; the reason is logical — privacy or protection |
